title: Dickinson v. Zurko (1999)
summary: The Administrative Procedure Act's standards for judicial review of agency factfinding govern the Federal Circuit's review of Patent and Trademark Office findings, so the stricter clearly erroneous standard used for trial court findings does not apply.
notes:
Key line: "The APA was meant to bring uniformity to a field full of variation and diversity." (Breyer, J.)

Citation: 527 U.S. 150 (1999).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Q. Todd Dickinson, Acting Commissioner of Patents and Trademarks, representing the Patent and Trademark Office. The respondents were Mary E. Zurko and her co-inventors, who had applied for a patent on a method for increasing computer security and had been refused. The Solicitor General argued for the Commissioner. Amici supporting the applicants included the Biotechnology Industry Organization, several intellectual property bar associations and the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, while intellectual property professors supported the Commissioner. The underlying disagreement was between the Federal Circuit, which had long reviewed PTO fact findings under a clearly erroneous standard, and the PTO, which argued that ordinary APA court agency review applied.
sections.Material Facts: Zurko and her co-inventors applied for a patent on a method of increasing computer security. The PTO examiner concluded that the method was obvious in light of the prior art and denied the application under 35 U.S.C. section 103, and the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences upheld the examiner. Section 706 of the APA, enacted in 1946, directs reviewing courts to set aside agency findings that are arbitrary, capricious or an abuse of discretion, or unsupported by substantial evidence in cases reviewed on the record of an agency hearing. Section 559 provides that the APA does not limit or repeal additional requirements recognized by law. The Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, the Federal Circuit's predecessor, had decided 89 pre-APA cases reviewing PTO decisions with phrases such as manifest error and clearly wrong, and the Federal Circuit treated that practice as an additional requirement preserved by section 559.
sections.Procedural History: The applicants sought review in the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. A panel treated the question of what the prior art teaches as one of fact and held the PTO's finding clearly erroneous, 111 F.3d 887 (1997). To resolve the standard of review controversy the Federal Circuit reheard the matter en banc and concluded that its stricter court to court standard was legally proper, 142 F.3d 1447 (1998). The Solicitor General petitioned for certiorari on behalf of the Commissioner, and the Supreme Court granted the writ to decide whether Federal Circuit review of PTO factfinding must take place within the framework of section 706. On June 10, 1999, the Court reversed and remanded by a vote of 6 to 3.
sections.Issue: Whether section 706 of the Administrative Procedure Act, with its arbitrary and capricious and substantial evidence standards for court review of agency factfinding, applies when the Federal Circuit reviews findings of fact made by the Patent and Trademark Office, or whether the pre-1946 practice of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals in reviewing PTO decisions under a clearly erroneous or manifest error standard was an additional requirement recognized by law that section 559 of the APA preserved, permitting the stricter court to court standard of review.
sections.Holding: The Court held that section 706 applies and that the Federal Circuit must use the APA framework when reviewing PTO findings of fact. The parties agreed that the PTO is an agency, that the finding was one of fact and that it was agency action, so APA standards govern unless an exception applies. The Federal Circuit's claimed exception under section 559 failed because the existence of an additional requirement must be clear, and the 89 pre-APA cases did not reflect a well established stricter court to court standard. The policy arguments about disruption to the patent bar, anomalies between direct appeals and district court actions, and the value of stricter review were unconvincing. The judgment was reversed and the case remanded.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Breyer explained that the APA was meant to bring uniformity to a field full of variation and diversity, so a grandfathered common law departure from its standards must be clear, just as section 559 requires later statutes to modify the APA expressly. The 89 CCPA cases used words such as clearly wrong and manifest error, but linguistic conventions were not settled before 1946, courts then sometimes used clearly erroneous to describe deferential agency review and substantial evidence to describe trial court review, and none of the 89 opinions used the terms of art clear error or clearly erroneous. Morgan v. Daniels, the foundation the Federal Circuit invoked, reasoned that review of a Patent Office decision was more than a mere appeal and required a standard weaker than appellate review of a trial court. The CCPA cases explained their deference by pointing to the PTO's expertise and to agreement between two agency tribunals, reasons traditionally given for deferring to agencies rather than to trial judges. On policy, the Court said it had never settled the matter, that creating section 559 precedent would itself be disruptive, and that the difference between the standards is subtle: the Court could not find a case where use of one rather than the other changed the outcome, and the basic reviewing task, applying logic and experience to a record, is similar under both. The APA still requires meaningful review rather than rubber stamping.

topics.lrs-n-substantial-evidence: Zurko distinguishes the APA’s agency review from clearly-erroneous review of judicial findings.
topics.lrs-i-law-fact: The case fixes the standard for judicial review of an agency's findings of fact (APA § 706 rather than court/court clearly-erroneous review), the fact half of the law/fact allocation.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3. Chief Justice Rehnquist dissented, joined by Justices Kennedy and Ginsburg. He argued that section 559 preserved additional requirements recognized by law in 1946 without any clear statement rule, that the APA raised minimum standards of review rather than lowering existing ones, and that the Court should have deferred to the unanimous en banc Federal Circuit, the specialized Article III court for patent appeals, and the patent bar, both of which read the 89 cases as recognizing the clearly erroneous standard as a requirement placed on the PTO.
